# Follow the Trace, Prove the Case {.unnumbered}

> The tool does not decide what happened. It produces an artefact. The investigator decides what the artefact can support.

## Who this is for

This book is for people learning digital forensics, incident responders who need to explain their findings, and analysts who can run a tool but are less sure how to defend the result.

It assumes you can use a command line, read a log and follow a lab. It does not assume you are a lawyer, a police officer or a full-time forensic examiner.

The same discipline applies to AI: follow the output back to its source until you can defend every claim.

## The companion lab

The running case is the **Cloudcore** investigation in the [forensics-docker-lab](https://forensics.borck.education/). A mid-sized software company suspects that an employee copied client data before leaving. The lab provides a USB image, a memory dump, an email archive, network traffic and report templates.

The lab teaches the tools. This book teaches the reasoning around them: what question you are answering, how to preserve the evidence, what an artefact can support and how to report uncertainty without weakening the case.

## What you will build

By the end, you will have a method for:

- framing an investigation as questions and hypotheses
- preserving integrity and documenting custody
- distinguishing acquisition from analysis
- examining disk, memory, email and network evidence
- correlating artefacts into a timeline without forcing a story
- writing a report that a decision-maker can use and an examiner can reproduce

## How to read it

Read the chapters in order. Each chapter ends with an AI exploration, a lab bridge, practice tasks, a summary and a reflection. The lab bridge points to the relevant part of the Docker lab, but the chapter stands alone if you only want the reasoning.

The case is deliberately not solved in the text. The evidence in your lab run is the evidence you must explain.
